content: Malaria is transmitted to humans through the bites of adult female Anopheles mosquitoes infected with Plasmodium parasites. Ivermectin, an anti-parasitic medication, has been shown to kill mosquitoes that feed on the blood of individuals who have ingested the drug. This mosquito-killing effect has been demonstrated in individual randomized trials, leading to interest in using ivermectin as a potential tool for malaria control. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of administering ivermectin at the community level on malaria transmission. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group (CIDG) Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, the Science Citation Index Expanded, the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) RePORTER database, up to January 14, 2021. Reference lists of included studies were also reviewed, and researchers in the field were contacted to identify unpublished or ongoing trials. The study included cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) that compared ivermectin, administered as single or multiple doses, with a control treatment or placebo in populations residing in malaria-endemic regions. The primary outcomes assessed were the prevalence of malaria parasite infection and the incidence of clinical malaria within the community. Two independent reviewers extracted data on the number of events and participants in each trial arm at the time of assessment. For rate data, the total time at risk in each trial arm was recorded. The risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane's RoB 2 tool for cRCTs. The methods of data analysis, adjustments for clustering or other covariates, and estimates of intra-cluster correlation (ICC) coefficients were documented. Trial data were re-analyzed to account for cluster effects using a Poisson mixed-effects model with small sample size correction and a cluster-level analysis with a linear weighted model. The review included one cRCT and identified six ongoing trials. The included cRCT was conducted in eight villages in Burkina Faso, which were randomized into two groups. Both groups received a single dose of ivermectin (150–200 µg/kg) along with albendazole. However, the intervention group received an additional five doses of ivermectin, administered every three weeks. Children aged five years and younger were enrolled in an active cohort and were repeatedly screened for malaria infection. The primary outcome was the cumulative incidence of uncomplicated malaria in this cohort over an 18-week study period. The study was judged to have a high risk of bias because the analysis did not account for clustering or correlations between participants within the same village. The results did not demonstrate a significant effect of ivermectin on the cumulative incidence of uncomplicated malaria in the cohort of children over the 18-week period (risk ratio 0.86, 95% confidence interval 0.62 to 1.17; P = 0.2607). The evidence was rated as very low certainty. In conclusion, based on the single trial published to date, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether community administration of ivermectin has an effect on malaria transmission.
